passages.text: From the Greek <italic>pseudo</italic> (“false”) + <italic>monas</italic> (“unit”). <sentence_start/>In 1894, German botanist Walter Migula coined the term <italic>Pseudomonas</italic> for a genus he described as, “Cells with polar organs of motility. <sentence_start/>Formation of spores occurs in some species, but it is rare.” Migula never clarified the etymology of the term. <sentence_start/>However, the description of <italic>Pseudomonas</italic> as “false unit” does not make much sense, and an alternative explanation posits that Migula “had not traced directly the Greek ancestry of the name, but had simply created the name <italic>Pseudomonas</italic> for the resemblance of the cells to those of the nanoflagellate <italic>Monas</italic> in both size and active motility.” <italic>Monas</italic> was coined by Danish naturist Otto Friedrich Müller in 1773 to describe a genus of “infusoria” characterized as “<italic>vermis inconspicuous</italic>, <italic>simplicissimus</italic>, <italic>pellucidus</italic>, <italic>punctiformis</italic>” (“inconspicuous worm, simple, transparent, tiny”).

<italic>Pseudomonas aeruginosa</italic> [adj. fem. of <italic>aerūginōsus</italic>] from Latin <italic>aerūgō</italic> (“copper rust or verdigris,” hence green) + -<italic>ōsus</italic> (added to a noun to form an adjective indicating an abundance of that noun) is named for the greenish-blue color of bacterial colonies. <sentence_start/>The organism has emerged as one of the most serious causes of nosocomial infections.

<italic>Suggested citation for this article</italic>: Etymologia: <italic>Pseudomonas</italic>. <sentence_start/>Emerg Infect Dis [serial on the Internet]. <sentence_start/>2012 Aug [<italic>date cited</italic>].
